title: Short Stuff: Sulfanilamide Disaster
summary: Short Stuff episode on the 1937 Elixir Sulfanilamide disaster. Josh and Chuck explain how Massengill's chief chemist Harold Watkins made a liquid form of sulfanilamide using diethylene glycol, a deadly solvent, and how the drug was sold untested. The AMA investigated, and FDA field agents struggled to locate salesmen, pharmacies and doctors to recall the roughly 240 gallons produced. The FDA used the mislabeling ("elixir" containing no alcohol) loophole under the 1906 Act to seize about 234 gallons. About 105 people died, including 34 children. The deaths led to the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act, championed by Senator Royal Copeland, who died days after its passage. Harold Watkins died by suicide.

segments.title: Opening banter and pronunciation
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck introduce the short episode on the sulfanilamide disaster and joke about how to pronounce sulfanilamide.

segments.title: Background and making the liquid elixir
segments.summary: Context on the 1906 Food and Drugs Act and the loosely regulated medicine market. Gerhard Domagk's sulfanilamide antibiotic is turned into a liquid by Massengill chief chemist Harold Watkins, who uses diethylene glycol as a solvent. The product is sweetened, colored pink, and flavored with raspberry.

segments.title: Toxicity and early deaths
segments.summary: Diethylene glycol is described as a deadly poison that destroys the kidneys, causing vomiting, seizures and intense pain. The product was sold without safety testing because the law did not require it. About 240 gallons were shipped in September 1937 and deaths were reported within weeks.

segments.title: AMA inquiry and FDA recall effort
segments.summary: The AMA investigated the deaths and requested the ingredient list from Massengill. FDA agents struggled to track down traveling salesmen, sales slips, pharmacies and doctors, who were reluctant to share information. The FDA pressed Massengill to recall the product.

segments.title: Mislabeling loophole and final toll
segments.summary: The FDA could not force a recall, but it seized the drug under the 1906 Act because it was mislabeled as an elixir despite containing no alcohol. About 234 of 240 gallons were recovered. Around 105 people died, including 34 children. Had the loophole not existed, the hosts say about 4,000 might have died. Harold Watkins died by suicide, and doctors and staff were left with guilt.

segments.title: Legislative aftermath and Senator Copeland
segments.summary: The public outcry pushed Congress to pass an update to the 1906 Act. Senator Royal Copeland of New York championed the bill and died of exhaustion four days after it passed. A doctor from Mount Olive wrote to President Roosevelt asking for more oversight.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts wrap up the episode and give the standard sign-off for Stuff You Should Know, produced by iHeartRadio.
